title: LCA in a BST
description: In a BST, walk down from root: if both p, q < root go left, both > root go right, else root IS the split point and therefore the LCA.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes `p` and `q` in a BST — the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants. A node can be a descendant of itself, so if `p` is an ancestor of `q`, then `p` IS the LCA."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Is the tree guaranteed to be a valid BST (no duplicates, strict ordering)? The BST property is the whole point of this problem.
• Are `p` and `q` guaranteed to exist in the tree? If not, what should I return — null?
• Can `p === q`? (LCA of a node and itself is just that node.)
• Should I return the node reference or just its value?
sections.why: The 'node is a descendant of itself' clause is the small print that determines whether the LCA can be `p` or `q` themselves. Missing it leads to a bug where you skip past the answer looking for something deeper. The 'guaranteed to be a BST' question matters because the whole O(h) trick depends on the ordering — without it you'd fall back to the generic-tree LCA algorithm, which is O(n).

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the generic-tree LCA — then leverage the BST property.
sections.say:
"For a generic binary tree (no BST property), the standard LCA is: recurse into left and right subtrees looking for p or q. If both sides return non-null, this node is the LCA. If only one side does, propagate that side up. That's O(n) time because you potentially visit every node.

But this is a BST, so I can do much better. The BST ordering tells me, without exploration, which subtree p and q are in: if both are less than the current node, both are in the left subtree, so the LCA is in the left subtree. Same logic on the right. The first node where they diverge — one less, one greater, or one equals the node itself — is the LCA. That's O(h) time, never branches into both subtrees, and is iterative with O(1) space."
sections.why: Naming the generic O(n) LCA first — and then explaining how the BST property cuts it to O(h) — is the move. It proves you can solve the harder generic version and chose the BST shortcut deliberately. Interviewers love when you show the optimization is enabled by problem structure, not by cleverness.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to descending toward the split point?
sections.say:
"The BST property gives us total ordering: every node 'partitions' its subtree into 'smaller on the left' and 'larger on the right'. For two target nodes p and q, exactly three things can happen at any node N during the descent:

(1) Both p.val < N.val and q.val < N.val → LCA is in N's left subtree (because both targets live there). Descend left.
(2) Both p.val > N.val and q.val > N.val → symmetric. Descend right.
(3) Otherwise — they split (one less, one greater), OR N equals one of them → N IS the LCA. Done.

Case (3) is the convergence: the moment p and q stop being on the same side of N is the moment N becomes their common ancestor with no deeper alternative. Iterative descent, O(h) time, O(1) space. This is fundamentally different from generic-tree LCA because BST ordering lets you pick ONE direction at each step instead of exploring both."
sections.why: The 'three cases' framing is the clean derivation. Saying 'the moment they stop being on the same side IS the LCA' is the key insight — it explains why the algorithm is correct, not just what it does. Naming 'descend toward the split point' as the technique distinguishes it from generic LCA, sliding-window two-pointers, or any other 'walk down the structure' pattern.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a clean split at the root, a case where one target IS the ancestor of the other, and a deeper split.

examples.note: Clean split at root — 2 < 6 and 8 > 6, so the root is the LCA immediately.
examples.trace: node=6: p=2, q=8 → 2 < 6 and 8 > 6 → split! return 6

examples.note: p is the ancestor of q — case where node equals one of the targets.
examples.trace:
node=6: p=2, q=4 → both < 6 → go left
node=2: p=2, q=4 → 2 equals node.val (not both <, not both >) → return 2 (node IS the LCA because p is ancestor of q)

examples.note: Deep split — both targets in the left subtree, LCA is deeper than the root.
examples.trace:
node=6: p=3, q=5 → both < 6 → go left
node=2: p=3, q=5 → both > 2 → go right
node=4: p=3, q=5 → 3 < 4 and 5 > 4 → split! return 4

sections.why: The middle trace (p=2, q=4) is the load-bearing one — it exercises the 'node equals one of the targets' case that's easy to mis-handle. A careless implementation might check 'both <' and 'both >' and then recurse on a null when neither matches, never returning the current node. The third trace shows the LCA can be arbitrarily deep, not just the root — defends the O(h) bound by showing it can equal the tree height.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• p === q (same node) → LCA is that node itself; the first iteration hits the 'split' branch trivially because p.val and q.val are equal, neither both-less nor both-greater holds.
• p is an ancestor of q (or vice versa) → the descent reaches p, p.val is not both-less or both-greater than itself, so we return p. ✓
• p and q both at the root → root is the LCA, first iteration returns it.
• Left-skewed tree (effectively a linked list) → O(n) descent worst case. Same as the generic tree's worst case, but this is unavoidable — it's the tree's height.
• Both targets in the deepest level on opposite sides → LCA is somewhere mid-tree, descent goes through the path that splits them.
• Null tree → returns null. ✓
• p or q not in the tree → if guaranteed they exist (per the problem), no concern. If not, we'd walk off the tree and return null, which the loop's `while (node)` guard handles.
• Duplicates — by BST definition (strict) there shouldn't be any, but if the problem allows them, the descent strategy still works if you pick one consistent side for equals."
sections.why: The p-is-ancestor-of-q case is the one most candidates miss — they assume the LCA must be strictly above both targets, when actually a node can be its own ancestor by the problem's definition. Calling it out and showing the trace handles it correctly is the senior signal. The skewed-tree O(n) callout shows you know the worst-case isn't always O(log n) just because we're in a BST.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(h) — each iteration descends one level, and we descend at most h times before hitting the split point. For a balanced BST that's O(log n); for a skewed BST it's O(n). The descent never branches into both subtrees, which is the whole win over generic-tree LCA.

Space is O(1) for the iterative version — just one `node` pointer. The recursive version would be O(h) for the call stack, so I'd go iterative for symmetry with the O(1) win.

If the tree weren't a BST — just a generic binary tree — I'd switch to the recursive 'return both p and q from below' approach: if both subtrees return non-null, the current node is the LCA. That's LeetCode 236. Same problem family, different ordering assumption, much different algorithm.

And if you wanted to find the LCA of more than two nodes in a BST, the same descent works — keep descending while ALL targets are on the same side; the first split or hit is the LCA."
sections.why: The 'O(h) descent, never both subtrees' is the right defense — it explains WHY this is faster than generic LCA, not just that it is. The LCA-236 callout proves you see the family: BST-LCA and generic-LCA are distinct templates that share the LCA concept. The multi-target extension is unprompted bonus that demonstrates the descent strategy generalizes — a real signal of pattern understanding.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the iterative BST LCA. At every step the current node is compared against both target values; the BST ordering tells you which single subtree to descend into.
trace: const { tree, p: pVal, q: qVal } = input;
if (!arr || arr.length === 0 || arr[0] == null) return null;
const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
const p = { val: pVal }, q = { val: qVal };
yield { line: 1, label: `enter lowestCommonAncestor — tree ${JSON.stringify(tree)}, p=${pVal}, q=${qVal}`, state: { treeShape: tree, p: pVal, q: qVal } };
yield { line: 2, label: `node = root (${node.val})`, state: { treeShape: tree, p: pVal, q: qVal, node: node.val } };
yield { line: 3, label: `loop — node=${node.val}, p=${p.val}, q=${q.val}`, state: { treeShape: tree, node: node.val, p: p.val, q: q.val } };
yield { line: 5, label: `both ${p.val} and ${q.val} < ${node.val} → go left`, state: { treeShape: tree, node: node.val, direction: 'left' } };
yield { line: 7, label: `both ${p.val} and ${q.val} > ${node.val} → go right`, state: { treeShape: tree, node: node.val, direction: 'right' } };
yield { line: 9, label: `split (or hit p/q) at ${node.val} — return ${node.val}`, state: { treeShape: tree, node: node.val, returns: node.val } };
yield { line: 11, label: 'walked off tree — return null', state: { treeShape: tree, returns: null } };

notes: BST ordering is the whole trick — you never need to search both subtrees like in a generic binary tree.
The first node where p and q diverge (one goes left, other right) OR equals one of them IS the LCA.
Iterative form is O(1) space; the recursive version is O(h) for the call stack.

questions.q: Why does the BST version beat the generic tree LCA?
options: BST ordering lets you pick ONE subtree at each step instead of searching both
Generic LCA does not work on BSTs

questions.q: When both p.val and q.val are greater than node.val, you go:

options: Both descendants are on the same side
p and q split (one goes left, one right) OR node equals p or q
O(h) where h is tree height

questions.q: If p = 2 is an ancestor of q = 4, what is their LCA?
options: 2 itself, because a node is considered a descendant of itself
questions.explain: By definition a node is a descendant of itself, so when the descent reaches 2 (neither both-less nor both-greater holds) it returns 2 as the LCA.

questions.q: Why is the descent O(h) and not O(n) like generic-tree LCA?
options: BST ordering lets it descend exactly one subtree per step, following a single root-to-split path instead of exploring both subtrees
It uses a hash map of ancestors
questions.explain: Each step picks one direction by comparing both targets to the node, so it walks at most one root-to-node path of length h — generic LCA must recurse into both subtrees, visiting up to all n nodes.

questions.q: Why don't you need to locate p and q in the tree first?
options: Because p and q are passed as indices
The split point depends only on comparing p.val and q.val against each node's value, so the LCA is found during a single descent
Because the tree is sorted into an array first
You actually must find them first
questions.explain: Knowing only p.val and q.val is enough — the BST ordering tells you which side each target lies on at every node, so the first divergence is the LCA without a separate search.

questions.q: What is the space complexity of the iterative form, and how does it compare to recursive?
options: O(1) iterative (one pointer), versus O(h) for the recursive call stack
questions.explain: The iterative loop holds a single node pointer for O(1) space; the recursive version pays O(h) for the call stack, so iterative is the strict space win.

questions.q: The O(h) algorithm assumes both p and q exist in the tree. If a target is absent (and inputs aren't guaranteed), what happens?
options: The descent can walk off the tree to null and the loop returns null
questions.explain: Comparisons still steer the descent, but with a missing target it may reach a null child; the while(node) guard then exits and returns null.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the iterative BST LCA. Tighten by going LEFT when both targets are smaller, RIGHT when both are larger.

blanks.hint: both targets smaller than the current node

L3.prompt: Write `lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q)` for a BST. Build [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5] and log the LCA of (2,8), (2,4), and (3,5) — each `.val` on its own line.
hints: Use the BST ordering — never recurse into both subtrees.
Loop while node is not null; split point (or hitting p/q) is the answer.
LCA(2,4) is 2 itself because 2 is an ancestor of 4.
